parole.significato: creates the female form of some persons or occupations, as English -ess
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch -esse, borrowed from Old Northern French -esse, from Late Latin -issa (as in abbātissa (“abbess”)).

parole.significato: abele; term used of certain poplars, mainly the white poplar (Populus alba), grey poplar (Populus × canescens) or black…
parole.testo: From Middle Dutch abeel, from Old Northern French abiel, from Latin albellus, a diminutive of albus (“white”).

From Middle Dutch canevas, from Old Northern French canevas, from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). The spelling was lated influenced by English canvas. Doublet of cannabis and hennep.
From Middle Dutch fluwijn, from Old Northern French *floïne (modern Picard floène, flouène), a variant of Old French foïne (modern French fouine), from Latin fāgīna (mūstēla) (“beech weasel”).
From Middle Dutch cabel, from Old Northern French cable, a variant of Old French chable, from Late Latin capulum.

From Middle Dutch cachtel, from earlier caftel, from Old Northern French captel, from Medieval Latin capitāle (“young cattle”), from Classical Latin capitālis (“of the head”), from caput (“head”) + -alis (“-al”). Cognate with English cattle.

From Middle Dutch campioen, from Old Northern French campion, campiun (cf. French champion), from Proto-West Germanic *kampijō (cf. German Kämpe), derived from *kamp (“field, fight”), from Latin campus.

From Middle Dutch canse, borrowed from Old Northern French caance (compare central cheance), from Vulgar Latin *cadentia, from cadere (“to fall”), referring to the falling of dice. Doublet of cadans, cadens, and sjans. Cognate with French chance, English chance.
From Middle Dutch cant, from Old Northern French cant, from Medieval Latin canthus.
From Middle Dutch carbonkel, from Old Northern French carbuncle, from Latin carbunculus.
From Middle Dutch castēel, from Old Northern French castel, from Latin castellum. Doublet of Kessel, chateau, Castilië, castellum, ketella, and telo.
From Middle Dutch calant (“person, friend”), from Old Northern French calant (compare regular Old French chalant), from Old French chaloir (“to heat, to care about”), from Latin caleō (“to be hot”).
From Middle Dutch planke, from Old Dutch *planka, from Old Northern French planke, from Late Latin planca.

From Middle Dutch schaers. From Old Northern French scars, escars ("sparing, niggard, parsimonious, miserly, poor"; > French échars, Medieval Latin scarsus (“diminished, reduced”)), of uncertain origin. From Middle Dutch schāetse (“stilt”), from Old Northern French escache (“a stilt, trestle”), from Frankish *skakkjā (“stilt”, literally “thing that moves”), from the verb *skakan (“to shake”).
